report:
## Research Summary

Your sister's belief is well-supported by evidence, though with some nuance.

**Strongest evidence:** The landmark 2016 NEJM randomized trial (Tuuli et al., n≈1,147) directly compared chlorhexidine-alcohol vs. iodine-alcohol skin prep before cesarean delivery and found chlorhexidine-alcohol produced a **significantly lower risk of surgical-site infection** (4.0% vs. 7.3%). This large, well-designed RCT is the primary basis for current practice recommendations (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1511048).

**Corroborating meta-analyses:** Multiple systematic reviews/meta-analyses pooling this and other RCTs generally support chlorhexidine's advantage. A 2018 systematic review and meta-analysis found chlorhexidine-alcohol associated with reduced SSI compared with povidone-iodine (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30184558/). A more recent network meta-analysis (RCTs through Feb 2024) found alcohol-based chlorhexidine had the **highest probability of being effective** at preventing SSI, though credible intervals overlapped with iodine-alcohol, indicating the certainty of superiority isn't absolute (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0195670124001282).

**Some caveats:** Not every individual trial found a statistically significant difference — a smaller pilot RCT reported a trend favoring chlorhexidine that didn't reach significance (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34404473/). This is typical of underpowered smaller trials; larger trials and pooled analyses more consistently favor chlorhexidine.

**Bottom line:** The claim reflects mainstream evidence-based obstetric practice. The best single trial (NEJM 2016) and most meta-analyses support chlorhexidine-alcohol as superior or at least non-inferior to iodine-alcohol for reducing post-cesarean SSI, which is why many hospital guidelines now recommend it. However, some overlap in confidence intervals across pooled analyses means the effect, while real, isn't overwhelming in magnitude.
